video_title: Liaquat Ahamed on Financial Crises, Gold, and the Lessons of 1873
gist: Tyler Cowen interviews Liaquat Ahamed on his book 1873, arguing the 1873 crisis was really a 20-year 'First Great Deflation' whose output damage was mild (flexible prices) but whose distributional and political damage was large, with Bismarck's destruction of French-anchored bimetallism as the root cause and South African gold rescuing the gold standard. They also cover sovereign debt enforcement (Gladstone's 40% stake in Egyptian bonds vs. Turkey's haircut), 1920s gold parity and Weimar hyperinflation, bubble diagnosis by rate of change, IMF politicization, and country outlooks (UK stagnation, India water risk, US innovation).

insights.claim: Ahamed argues the 1873 crisis did not cause a deep depression but triggered a ~20-year deflation whose main damage was to political economy rather than output; he says a better title for his book would be 'The First Great Deflation'.
insights.speaker: Liaquat Ahamed
insights.so_what: Judge crises by distributional/political fallout, not just GDP drawdown.
insights.quote: A better title would have been The First Great Deflation.

insights.claim: Despite deflation, the major economies grew roughly 2.5% a year for 20 years after 1873, which Ahamed attributes to flexible prices and falling nominal wages.
insights.speaker: Liaquat Ahamed
insights.so_what: Price/wage flexibility lets real economies absorb deflation; rigid modern wages make deflation far more dangerous.
insights.quote: Because prices were flexible. Nominal wages went down.

insights.claim: Ahamed holds that the distributional and political consequences of the post-1873 deflation were more damaging than the pure economic consequences.
insights.speaker: Liaquat Ahamed
insights.so_what: Deflation transfers wealth debtor-to-creditor and breeds political backlash even when growth holds up.
insights.quote: I think the distributional consequences and the political impact of those distributional consequences were much more damaging than the pure economic consequences.

insights.claim: Half of the 1873-1896 period was classified as recessionary, so growth was highly unstable even though the average rate was decent.
insights.speaker: Liaquat Ahamed
insights.so_what: Good long-run averages can mask violent cyclicality that matters for leveraged investors.
insights.quote: Half the period from 1873 to 1896 was classified as recessionary.

insights.claim: Cowen notes US per-capita growth in the period is estimated at only 1.7-1.8% and suggests hedonic mismeasurement understates true growth; Ahamed agrees the era truly transformed the United States.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Official growth stats likely understate transformative technology eras, relevant to judging today's AI-era productivity data.
insights.quote: No question that it truly transformed the United States.

insights.claim: Ahamed's biggest revision from his research: the depression portion was not severe and economic growth was surprisingly resilient, but societies became deeply fractured and mid-Victorian liberalism went into retreat.
insights.speaker: Liaquat Ahamed
insights.so_what: Political fragmentation, not output loss, is the lasting legacy of deflationary shocks.
insights.quote: Surprisingly, the economic growth was surprisingly resilient.

insights.claim: Ahamed says the post-1873 fracturing of political economy laid the foundations for many problems that afflicted the global economy in the early 20th century.
insights.speaker: Liaquat Ahamed
insights.so_what: Long-lag political effects of monetary regimes can surface decades later.
insights.quote: It laid the foundations for many of the things that afflicted the global economy in the early part of the 20th century.

insights.claim: The post-1873 era brought US populism, resurgent European protectionism, retreat from liberal ideas, and revived British imperialism (the invasion of Egypt and the scramble for Africa).
insights.speaker: Liaquat Ahamed
insights.so_what: Deflationary eras correlate with protectionism and populism — a pattern worth watching in any prolonged disinflationary squeeze.
insights.quote: it’s populism in the United States, the resurgence of protectionism in Europe, the retreat from liberal ideas, the revival of imperialism by Britain when it invaded Egypt.

insights.claim: The 1873 crisis and subsequent monetary decisions broke Republican dominance: Democrats returned in the 1874 congressional election, nearly won the presidency in 1876, and the resulting deal ended Reconstruction, with a line traceable to Jim Crow.
insights.speaker: Liaquat Ahamed
insights.so_what: Financial crises and monetary choices can reshape political control for a generation.
insights.quote: The 1873 depression or crisis and the subsequent monetary policy decisions set that back.

themes.theme: Bimetallism, Bismarck and the gold standard

insights.claim: Ahamed names Bismarck the biggest villain of the era: he imposed a giant reparation bill on France that disrupted European financial markets and destroyed the stable bimetallic monetary system.
insights.speaker: Liaquat Ahamed
insights.so_what: Geopolitically motivated monetary regime changes can trigger multi-decade deflation.
insights.quote: The biggest villain in my whole book is Bismarck.

insights.claim: France, holding the largest stock of precious-metal reserves, acted as the linchpin of bimetallism and stabilized gold and silver prices until 1873; destroying that system initiated the deflation, per Ahamed.
insights.speaker: Liaquat Ahamed
insights.so_what: A single reserve-rich stabilizer can anchor a multi-asset monetary system; its removal is deflationary.
insights.quote: By destroying that system, he, I think, initiated the deflation

insights.claim: Ahamed argues bimetallism is stable with a stabilizing central bank, and that central banks collectively could have held gold and silver prices through the 1880s-1890s silver supply surge by shifting holdings into gold.
insights.speaker: Liaquat Ahamed
insights.so_what: Pegs between commodity monies can survive supply shocks if reserve holders coordinate.
insights.quote: Not if you have a stabilizing central bank.

insights.claim: Cowen counters that bimetallism tends to collapse into monometallism and most currency pegs eventually fail when central banks run out of reserves or credibility.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Default skepticism on long-lived pegs remains warranted.
insights.quote: Most currency pegs don’t last for that long.

insights.claim: During the gold drought of the 1870s-1880s the gold standard was an ever-tightening vice on global money supply; Ahamed thinks another decade of falling prices might have pushed the US onto silver.
insights.speaker: Liaquat Ahamed
insights.so_what: Monetary base growth constrained by a scarce commodity produces chronic deflation and political pressure to abandon the regime.
insights.quote: it looked as if the gold standard was becoming a sort of ever-tightening vice on the global money supply.

insights.claim: South African gold discoveries essentially bailed out and saved the gold standard, ending the impetus for bimetallism.
insights.speaker: Liaquat Ahamed
insights.so_what: Supply shocks to a monetary commodity can rescue or doom a monetary regime.
insights.quote: I think the South African gold discoveries essentially saved the gold standard.

insights.claim: Silver-standard countries like India and China devalued against gold currencies and experienced no deflation, but their currencies could not serve as reserve assets.
insights.speaker: Liaquat Ahamed
insights.so_what: Devaluation trades away reserve-currency status for domestic price stability.
insights.quote: There was no deflation in India. There was no deflation in China

insights.claim: Had the US adopted silver, Ahamed believes it would have delayed the development of the US as a major financial market.
insights.speaker: Liaquat Ahamed
insights.so_what: Hard-money choices shaped the dollar's eventual reserve role.
insights.quote: If the US had become a silver currency, I think it would have delayed the development of the US as a major financial market.

insights.claim: Ahamed says a global bimetallic system can work with individual countries on gold or silver, as in roughly 1820-1870, provided key central banks stabilize the gold-silver price; he claims the people in charge in the 19th century had no clue how the system worked.
insights.speaker: Liaquat Ahamed
insights.so_what: Monetary stability depended on a few anchor institutions, not universal adoption.
insights.quote: Essentially, all of the people in charge had no clue how the system worked.

themes.theme: Sovereign debt: Gladstone, Egypt and Turkey

insights.claim: Gladstone put about 40% of his net worth into Egyptian bonds yielding 12-14% at their peak; after Britain invaded Egypt, it insisted on repayment at par, so investors got roughly 90-100 cents on the dollar.
insights.speaker: Liaquat Ahamed
insights.so_what: Distressed sovereign debt backed by a creditor power's enforcement can be extraordinarily lucrative.
insights.quote: Gladstone had put 40 percent of his net worth into Egyptian bonds.

insights.claim: Turkey, owing more than Egypt, used its geostrategic importance as a bulwark against Russia to get its debt halved and then restructured again, paying perhaps 30 cents on the dollar, while Egypt got a raw deal.
insights.speaker: Liaquat Ahamed
insights.so_what: Sovereign recovery rates depend on geopolitical leverage, not just ability to pay.
insights.quote: they managed to negotiate to have their debt cut in half, so 50 cents on the dollar.

insights.claim: Cowen frames Gladstone as trading on inside information rather than invading for profit, likening it to what might be found inside parts of the Trump administration; Ahamed agrees Gladstone believed full repayment was moral.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Policymakers' positions can front-run policy; insider-linked trades are a recurring signal.
insights.quote: He simply was trading on inside information, the way you might find today inside parts of the Trump administration.

insights.claim: With prices falling, a 14% nominal yield on Egyptian bonds implied an even higher real return, making it a brilliant investment.
insights.speaker: Liaquat Ahamed
insights.so_what: In deflation, high nominal yields from an enforceable obligor are exceptional real returns.
insights.quote: it was a brilliant investment.

themes.theme: Interwar money: the 1920s and fiat feasibility

insights.claim: Ahamed calls Britain's return to the prewar gold parity defensible, but argues a collective ~50% revaluation of gold to reflect WWI inflation would have instantly expanded global reserves and eased 1920s constraints.
insights.speaker: Liaquat Ahamed
insights.so_what: Revaluing the reserve asset is a policy lever to relieve global liquidity constraints.
insights.quote: with the stroke of a pen, increased the availability of global reserves and eliminated many of the constraints of the 1920s.

insights.claim: Ahamed thinks Britain going fully fiat in the 1920s would have caused a global financial crisis because investor confidence would not have allowed it.
insights.speaker: Liaquat Ahamed
insights.so_what: Fiat credibility is historically contingent on investor trust.
insights.quote: Oh, I think it would have been a global financial crisis.

insights.claim: Ahamed says any country with credibility could run fiat money, and argues the post-1945 system was effectively fiat; he doubts the gold link actually constrained the US in the 1950s-60s, while Cowen thinks it did until Nixon.
insights.speaker: Liaquat Ahamed
insights.so_what: The dollar's gold link may have mattered less than assumed, so its absence need not imply instability.
insights.quote: Could we have had a global fiat currency system? I think we did after ’45.

insights.claim: Ahamed's most plausible explanation for Weimar hyperinflation is that Germany let it run to convince creditors it could not pay reparations, since it was not revenue-maximizing.
insights.speaker: Liaquat Ahamed
insights.so_what: Sovereigns may deliberately damage their currency as a negotiating tactic against external creditors.
insights.quote: the only way that we will get out of paying reparations is if they realize that it’ll destroy our financial system, which they did.

insights.claim: Schacht stabilized the German currency, presided over a late-1920s boom financed by heavy US borrowing, resigned when the Depression hit, then ran a second 'economic miracle' under Hitler using controls and import quotas with no reserves.
insights.speaker: Liaquat Ahamed
insights.so_what: Capital controls and quotas can sustain a rearmament boom when reserves and trade collapse.
insights.quote: He presided over a second “economic miracle,”

themes.theme: Bubbles, debt restructuring and the IMF

insights.claim: Ahamed says a mania should be judged by the rate of price change, not just the level; pre-2008 Ireland, the US and Spain showed unsustainable price gains and people buying multiple houses.
insights.speaker: Liaquat Ahamed
insights.so_what: Use rate-of-change and speculative multi-unit buying, not valuation level alone, to diagnose bubbles.
insights.quote: A bubble has both to do with the level, but also the rate of change.

insights.claim: Cowen argues that, like railroads, Ireland's housing boom built needed homes and was arguably not big enough ex post given today's high prices and scarcity; Ahamed distinguishes building homes from trading existing ones.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Overbuilding booms can leave durable assets; supply-constrained markets may vindicate 'bubble' prices.
insights.quote: They didn’t have a big enough bubble, ex post.

insights.claim: Both agree railroad financiers who funded three US boom-bust cycles were heroes because the country got a fantastic transport network; Cowen draws the parallel to today's AI builders.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Capex booms can destroy investor capital while creating lasting social value — an analog for AI infrastructure spending.
insights.quote: They’re the good guys in the story, just like the people today building AI.

insights.claim: Ahamed would stop the IMF from yielding to US pressure to lend to unsustainable countries, saying the US uses the IMF for foreign policy goals, a pattern Cowen links to Pakistan's 23-24 bailouts.
insights.speaker: Liaquat Ahamed
insights.so_what: Repeat IMF programs for geopolitically important borrowers signal politically driven, not credit-driven, lending.
insights.quote: The US has used the IMF as a vehicle for foreign policy objectives which essentially distort the IMF’s very reasonable economic practices.

insights.claim: Ahamed says the flaw in both the eurozone crisis and the US housing bust was failure to restructure unpayable debts, and Europe lacked a hegemon, with Germany too reluctant, to allocate restructuring costs.
insights.speaker: Liaquat Ahamed
insights.so_what: Debt overhangs persist absent a hegemon willing to apportion losses.
insights.quote: We should have found a better way to have restructured those debts.

insights.claim: Ahamed agrees the UK is stuck, with little real wage or productivity growth since 2008, and finds it puzzling given how many AI inventors were British.
insights.speaker: Liaquat Ahamed
insights.so_what: UK talent generation fails to translate into domestic capture of innovation value.
insights.quote: One of the striking things is how many inventors of AI were British.

insights.claim: Ahamed is not optimistic about India due to environmental damage, water problems and authorities' inability to address them.
insights.speaker: Liaquat Ahamed
insights.so_what: Water and environmental constraints are an underpriced risk to the India growth story.
insights.quote: I’m not very optimistic about India because of the environmental damage and because of the water problems

insights.claim: Ahamed is optimistic about the US, expecting its inherent innovation to carry it through a downturn in its political fortunes, and praises France as remarkably innovative with possibly more startups than most of Europe.
insights.speaker: Liaquat Ahamed
insights.so_what: Innovation capacity is his core reason for US optimism; France underrated as a startup hub.
insights.quote: the inherent innovation that is coming out of the United States will see us through.

insights.claim: Ahamed became disillusioned with think tanks because since about 2016 so little policy has been driven by great ideas.
insights.speaker: Liaquat Ahamed
insights.so_what: Policy is less idea-driven, so expect political rather than technocratic outcomes.
insights.quote: That since then, for the last 10 years, so little policy is driven by great ideas.

insights.claim: Ahamed's possible next book is the 1971 collapse of Bretton Woods.
insights.speaker: Liaquat Ahamed
insights.so_what: Regime-change episodes in the dollar system remain a live focus for monetary historians.
insights.quote: the one that I’ve stumbled across is the ’71 collapse of Bretton Woods.
